title: U.S.-China Investments Can Still Work for Americans
text:
U.S.-China Investments Can Still Work for Americans

Foreign Policy

WANG Zhao/AFP/Getty Images

The following excerpt is from an op-ed published in Foreign Policy on November 12, 2026, written by Lizzi C. Lee, Fellow on Chinese Economy at ASPI's Center for China Analysis, and Fengming Lu, an assistant professor in the Coral Bell School of Asia Pacific Affairs at the Australian National University.The Board of Trade and Board of Investment, the mechanisms for negotiating tariff reductions and cross-border investment, respectively, were meant to turn the 2025 Busan summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping into concrete economic deliverables. So far, only the Board of Trade has developed an agenda, reflecting how difficult cross-border investment has become amid U.S.-China strategic rivalry.The Board of Investment could take the easy route of approving a handful of small, nonsensitive deals. Or it could aim higher, pursuing investments that deliver meaningful gains for both countries.China faces weak demand and fierce competition in its electric-vehicle sector at home. The United States needs more affordable green autos and stronger domestic capabilities in next-generation automotive technologies. At least in theory, some well-designed investment partnerships could help address both sides’ challenges.Read the full op-ed here.
